comment: Demo video (T-012). Each scene is a slide from slides.html or a cut of the app recording between two marks written by record_app.py. Narration is spoken as written: spell out abbreviations that should not be read as words.

scenes.narration: Emergency doctors sign orders under time pressure. Most prescribing checks look at drug pairs and coded data; the ones we looked at don't read the free-text note. And clinicians override between half and over ninety percent of medication alerts.

Take this synthetic patient: chest pain, on daily aspirin, and a note that says suspected acute coronary syndrome. The order is dexketoprofen, an anti-inflammatory. The coded record is still empty, so the rules alone find no issue.
This is what Open Med Check is for. Gemma 4 reads the note, and reviewed rules decide.
Here is the app. We open bed three, and fill in the test prescription.
Gemma reads the note and quotes it. The rules decide from those quotes: blocked, with the doctor's own words as the evidence, and an alternative the rules have already re-checked.
One click re-checks paracetamol: no issue found by these checks. The prescriber still decides.
Every quote is checked word for word against the note. The model can raise a verdict, never lower it. And if the model is down or answers badly, the card says the free-text note was not checked.

On seventy-six synthetic cases we wrote ourselves, a development set and not a clinical validation: seventy-two percent with the rules alone, ninety-seven percent with Gemma, and no false alarm on the thirty-four cases that should stay silent.

Gemma 4 is open-weight, so it can run on a hospital's own G P U, and the note never has to leave the building. We think the buyer is the medication-safety team, paying for a maintained rule table, integration and support. That is a hypothesis we have yet to test.
Today, Open Med Check is a demonstrator on synthetic patients, not a medical device. The next step we're looking for is a clinical pilot with a hospital pharmacy. It's open source, on GitHub.
